title: Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL)
prompt: Design a service that converts long URLs into short links and redirects users from a short link to the original URL. Assume it must serve a large, read-heavy global audience.
blurb: The classic read-heavy KV design — key generation, collisions, cache, CDN, and analytics.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (shorten, redirect, analytics, expiry, custom alias) from non-functional (low-latency redirect, high availability, durability).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about scale, read/write ratio, custom aliases, link lifetime/expiry, analytics needs.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Derives QPS (reads vs writes), storage/year, key length from cardinality, cache size.

rubric.label: API design
rubric.description: POST /shorten, GET /{code} redirect (301 vs 302 reasoning), analytics endpoints.

rubric.label: Data model
rubric.description: code→url mapping plus created_at, owner, expiry; choice of store.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: LB → stateless app tier → KV store + cache + CDN for redirects; write vs read paths.

rubric.label: Key generation depth
rubric.description: Base62 counter vs hashing vs KGS; collision handling; distributed counter / hot key.

rubric.label: Scaling
rubric.description: Sharding the KV store, replication, caching hot links, CDN edge redirects.

rubric.label: Bottlenecks
rubric.description: Identifies + mitigates cache hot path and the ID generator as a potential SPOF.

rubric.label: Reliability
rubric.description: Replication, failover, graceful degradation, backpressure on write path.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Redirect metrics, latency SLOs, click analytics pipeline, alerting.

rubric.label: Security & abuse
rubric.description: Malicious-URL scanning, rate limiting, auth for custom aliases, open-redirect avoidance.

functional_requirements: Create a short code for a long URL
clarifying_questions: How long must codes remain valid?

estimations.traffic: 100M new URLs/day ≈ 1.2K writes/s; ~100:1 read ratio ≈ 120K reads/s
estimations.cache: Cache hot 20% of daily reads in memory; ~tens of GB

data_model: urls(code PK, long_url, created_at, owner_id, expires_at)
api_design: POST /api/shorten { url, alias?, ttl? } → { code, short_url }
GET /{code} → 302 redirect (302 keeps analytics; 301 is cacheable but loses per-click counts)
reference.high_level_design: Writes go LB → app → KGS assigns base62 id → persist to sharded KV + warm cache. Reads go LB/CDN → cache → KV; redirect served from edge when possible. Analytics events streamed async to a queue → aggregation store.

deep_dives.probe: How do you generate codes without collisions at 1.2K writes/s across many app servers? Counter vs hash vs a key-generation service?
If you use a counter, how do you avoid a single point of contention — ranges/blocks per server? What happens on server crash mid-block?
What do you cache and with what eviction? How do you handle a stampede when a viral link's cache entry expires?
You store mappings in a database. How would you capture changes to feed the analytics/search pipeline — change data capture, something like Debezium, or dual writes?
301 vs 302 — what are the caching and analytics tradeoffs?

followup_bank.question: Eviction policy — TTL vs LRU? And how do you prevent a cache stampede?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions database or postgres or sql
followup_bank.question: How do you capture DB changes downstream — CDC/Debezium vs dual writes?
How do you handle hash collisions, and how long must the code be for your key space?
How is that counter distributed and made fault-tolerant across servers?

scaling: Shard KV by code prefix / consistent hashing
Read replicas + cache for hot links
CDN edge redirects for the hottest links
Async analytics to avoid slowing redirects
bottlenecks: Analytics write amplification on redirect path
tradeoffs: Counter (dense, predictable) vs hash (no coordination, collision risk)
Strong vs eventual consistency for analytics
alternative_solutions: Pre-generated key pool served by a KGS
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer scopes read-heavy traffic, estimates QPS/storage, picks a base62 key strategy with an explicit collision/coordination story, separates read/write paths with a cache + CDN for redirects, streams analytics asynchronously, and proactively raises the ID generator as the main SPOF plus cache stampede as the main hot-path risk.

interviewer_notes: Let the candidate drive requirements first. If they place a datastore, interrupt with the CDC/Debezium probe. If they add a cache, probe eviction + stampede. Push on key generation depth — this separates mid from senior. Reserve the last minutes for reliability + analytics pipeline.
